newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: Rare display of opposition in Uzbek capital.
newsitem.headline: Rare display of opposition in Uzbek capital.

text.p: In a rare display of opposition to Uzbek president Islam Karimov, about 300 people gathered outside a court in central Tashkent in support of an Islamic cleric fighting the government in a legal battle over his home.
Several women spoke in protest over the government's closure in 1995 of the Tokhtobou mosque and the medresa, or religious school, where the cleric, Abid Khan Nazarov, used to work.
Eyewitnesses said the crowd, watched by a small number of security officials, dispersed peacefully after the court case was adjourned due to the judge's ill health.
After the mosque was closed, Nazarov was evicted from his flat in the Uzbek capital while a new home promised him failed to materialise. He has challenged the government in court.
Mutabar Akhmedov, a member of human rights group Amnesty International, told Reuters the government would refuse to give Nazarov a replacement home.
"Today the second (court) hearing should have taken place," Akhmedov said. "I think the result of this business has already been decided (in the government's favour)," he said.
President Karimov, the largely desert nation's former Communist Party boss, fears Islamic fundamentalism among the 23 million population, who have been hit hard by tough economic changes.

He has tried to place Islam under the control of a Soviet-style "spiritual board", particularly in the Ferghana valley where Islam has deep roots. The valley also borders neighbouring Tajikistan where that government has waged a four-year civil war with Islamic guerrillas.
The Uzbek government closed a further two Tashkent medresas in February this year, leaving no openly functioning religious schools in the capital.
But according to official figures, the number of mosques since independence in 1991 has grown from 80 to 5,000.

Karimov, along with other Central Asian leaders, has also been unnerved by the rise of the purist Islamic Taleban militia in Afghanistan, urging support for anti-Taleban factions in the country to prevent a Taleban advance northwards towards the Uzbek-Afghan border.
